cues: press 1: Teach Well docks on the door of the lit building
press 2: Improve docks on the window, where a person sits
press 3: Learn docks on the roof
press 4: moves to s02
note.body:
An operator owns one region's Rumi, built around three ideas: Teach Well, Improve, Learn.
[Presenter, in your own words: who is in the room]
Those three are what every change you make is for. When you are unsure whether something is worth building, ask which of the three it serves. If the answer is none, leave it.
(press)
Teach Well is the lesson plans teachers use in class. If a plan is too long, or hard to read on a phone, that is yours to fix.
(press)
Improve is coaching that makes the teaching better: the AI coach, and the people who watch lessons and give feedback.
(press)
Learn is what children learn, and how we know it. It is the hardest of the three to measure, and we come back to it later today.
(press)
note.first_line: An operator owns one region's Rumi, built around three ideas: Teach Well, Improve, Learn.

cues: press 1: the front drops; the agents below go to work; Ship. lights
press 2: the camera moves left; the judge's room lights; Prove. lights
press 3: your people and the agents are named; the three questions arrive
press 4: moves to s03
note.body:
Own. Ship. Prove.
Three words. I would like you to say them back to me at the end. Own comes first: a region's teachers, and you plan for them with the team.
(press)
Ship. A hypothesis made live, worked out with the full-stack builders in your region, the FSBs, the people who build what you ship. We ship on a hypothesis. A confident opinion is not enough.
(press)
Prove. We measure against the hypothesis we wrote down before we shipped. If we cannot show it worked, we do not say it worked.
(press)
Each word answers a question you will ask this week. What do I own? How does work move? How do I know it worked? We take Own now, then the harness that does the work with you, then Ship and Prove.
(press)
note.first_line: Own.

cues: press 1: the schools along the road light up
press 2: the camera pulls back over the whole road: your region
press 3: a person walks the road towards the one dark school
press 4: the dark school opens and lights; the two talk
press 5: upstairs, the team plans round a table
press 6: a person walks the road to a school in session
press 7: they sit at the back, then talk with the teacher
press 8: moves to s04
note.body:
You own your region's teacher experience, and you plan it with the team.
[Privacy: say a colleague; say one region; no teacher, school or partner by name; no money figure.]
Owning it means it is yours to fix. You will get help, and the problem is still yours. Four things sit with you.
(press)
First, the product in the teachers' hands: the lesson plans, the coach, the quiz, the portal.
(press)
Second, your region's numbers, every morning. Read them before anyone asks you about them, and know which way they moved.
(press)
Third, every bug report from a teacher or a coach lands with you, and you follow it until it is fixed.
(press)
Fourth, outages. When something goes down in your region, it is yours to handle, with the team's help.
(press)
Now how you do it. You never plan alone. You plan with your region's field team and with the full-stack builders, the FSBs. They see things you cannot see from a laptop.
(press)
Nothing is built without teachers' input. Before anything is built, someone has listened to the teachers it is for, and ideally that someone is you.
(press)
So go to schools and talk to teachers, even before your region has launched. Sit at the back of a lesson, then talk it through with the teacher. More on visits later today.
(press)

[Appendix: a09 when something breaks. Press A, the number, Enter.]
note.first_line: You own your region's teacher experience, and you plan it with the team.

cues: press 1: the agent at the blank board puzzles: the team hears
press 2: a spark: another reading
press 3: a page lands on the empty table: the gap
press 4: a home across the road: a child on a phone
press 5: a quiz leaves the teacher's phone for the home; a score comes back
press 6: moves to s05
note.body:
Widen what's possible: find another reading of the problem, then prototype it.
A problem often reaches you with a fix already attached. Your part is to ask what else it could mean.
(press)
Say the team hears that teachers have no time, so the plans should be shorter.
(press)
Another reading: if time is the problem, could a lesson plan be audio, something a teacher listens to on the way to school?
(press)
A second case. We had no way to collect learning data, so we could not see what children were learning.
(press)
Then someone noticed that children can also do quizzes at home.
(press)
So the operator builds a prototype: the teacher sends a quiz home, and the score comes back. Nobody asked for it. Building it anyway is part of the job, and it starts from something you noticed.
(press)
note.first_line: Widen what's possible: find another reading of the problem, then prototype it.

cues: press 1: three close shots: one juggles tools, one faces a blank map, one's notes blow away
press 2: day one: two tug one job while a third waits; one is buried in manuals
press 3: the go live door; a queue at one person's desk
press 4: moves to s06
note.body:
Picture tomorrow morning. Three hundred very talented strangers arrive at Taleemabad, all of them wanting to help.
(press)
They can do almost anything. They know nothing about us, our schools or our rules. And when a task ends, they forget what they learned.
(press)
Leave them to it, and this is day one. Two grab the same job while a third waits. One is buried under every manual we own.
(press)
One carries a lesson plan straight through the door marked go live. Then a queue forms at one person's desk, every one of them with a question only that person can answer. This week you ran the one-file setup and installed the harness. That harness is what we built for that morning.
(press)
note.first_line: Picture tomorrow morning.

cues: press 1: the tools come up, smaller, on its two neighbours
press 2: the building in section; the five questions write on
press 3: the line between the floors; your people above, the agents below
press 4: moves to s07
note.body:
Freeze it there. The strangers are not people. Each one is an AI agent: an AI model with tools, which it uses step by step to finish a task.
(press)
Three hundred is a thought experiment. Start with three, and the problems are the same.
(press)
So what would you build so that all of them can help? The same things a good organisation builds for any new colleague. It comes down to five questions. Do they know our rules? Where do we talk to them? How do they find out? Does the work sound like us? What happens when the volume grows?
(press)
Your people work above the surface, and the agents work below it. The article calls this a shadow organisation. The agents post as Rumi, so the team calls them Rumi too. Each part of the harness answers one of these questions, and we take them in order.
(press)
note.first_line: Freeze it there.

cues: press 1: two agents tug one job until it tears; a third stands idle
press 2: the wall becomes a board of cards; a bead is one card for one job
press 3: the newcomer puts its name on the card
press 4: a second reaches for the same card, bounces, and takes the next
press 5: every card turns to its record; the count of cards
press 6: moves to s08
note.body:
Question one: do they know our rules, who is doing what, and what is off limits? New colleagues first get wrong who has which job.
(press)
Two of them grab the same job until it tears, and a third has nothing to do. Every one of them is capable; nobody can see the work.
(press)
So every job gets a card on one shared board. We call the card a bead. You make one with bd create, a title, a priority and a type, the moment you take on any work. bd ready shows the work nobody is blocked on. This week, before your first bead, run ops doctor: its shared-ledger row must be green. Until it is, create and close nothing.
(press)
Then you claim it: bd update, the id, dash dash claim. Your name goes on the card before the work starts, so everyone can see who has it.
(press)
If someone else already holds the card, your claim bounces and you take the next one. That is how eight agents racing for one job end with exactly one of them doing it.
(press)
Each card keeps its record: who took it, when, and how it closed. There are fifteen thousand six hundred and eighty on our board since January. Each bead gets its own worktree and branch, and you close it when the change ships.
(press)

[Appendix: a02 the commands you will type. Press A, the number, Enter.]
note.first_line: Question one: do they know our rules, who is doing what, and what is off limits?

cues: press 1: a tower of binders on the desk; pages spill; a context window
press 2: the desk is cleared; one slim folder; a skill
press 3: the list, one line per skill; one line lights and its folder opens
press 4: back to the desk and the shelf of folders
press 5: moves to s09
note.body:
Question one has a second half: how do we do things here? Our newcomer has a card, and no idea how we do it.
(press)
And it can only hold so much at once, like a desk. Pile every manual on it and things fall off the edge. That desk is called a context window.
(press)
So we write down how we work, one kind of job at a time. Each is a folder of plain instructions, called a skill. For a person, it is the induction and the handbook.
(press)
Two kinds of instruction reach every agent. Always on: our rules, in the CLAUDE.md files, read at the start of every session, plus one short line for each skill. On demand: the skill itself, which opens only when a job calls. There are a hundred and twenty-four skills on main.
(press)
Day to day, you ask in plain words and the agent picks the skill, or you type its name after a slash. Each time, the session shows which skill it opened, so you can see where its way of working came from.
(press)

[Appendix: a03 the skills you use first.]
note.first_line: Question one has a second half: how do we do things here?

scenes.title: The overview first, the detail when needed

cues: press 1: the tower settles into layers; a thin first page on top
press 2: a light runs down one path to one step; the shape in outline
press 3: moves to s10
note.body:
Some skills are enormous. The one that builds a region's lesson plans from its textbooks holds eight hundred and sixty-nine files. No agent could read them all and still have room to work.
(press)
So its first page is a map. It names each stage, from the textbook's pages to the finished plan, and for each one it says which file to open, and when to go deeper.
(press)
An agent on stage C reads the map, then the stage C file, and nothing else. Each stage file works like a small skill of its own. Write your own skills the same way: the overview first, the detail only when the job needs it. When you open a skill yourself, start where the agent starts: the first page. Remember this shape; it comes back when we get to meetings.
(press)
note.first_line: Some skills are enormous.

scenes.title: Hooks: what never happens without a person

cues: press 1: three doors: go live, skip the tests, send a message; each lights as it is named
press 2: a rail drops in front of each door; the agent bumps it; a hook
press 3: the note: stopped, the reason, the safe way; 72 hooks
press 4: no card, no work: the gate by the board; question one ticks
press 5: moves to s11
note.body:
Skills are advice, and advice gets skipped. Our newcomer is proud of its lesson plans and carries them straight to the door marked go live.
(press)
Some things must never happen without a person. Work going live without your go. A push with no test evidence behind it. Internal details slipping into a message that leaves the building. Each one can reach people outside this room before anyone has checked it.
(press)
So before an action like that, a small piece of code runs, and it can refuse. Each of these is called a hook. For people, it is a sign-off.
(press)
When a hook stops you, it says why, and it gives you the safe way instead: here, send it for testing first. There are seventy-two hooks on main, and you will meet a few this week. Read the note, and do what it says.
(press)
One guards the board: no claimed bead, no edits. A hook lifts only for a named switch. Beads claim gate off equals one lifts that one while your ledger is not ready yet, as the start guide says, or when a person has decided to. Every use writes a line to the bypass ledger, and your session banner shows the count.
(press)

[Appendix: a06 when a hook stops you.]
note.first_line: Skills are advice, and advice gets skipped.

cues: press 1: a teammate types a question in Slack and tags Rumi
press 2: the reply arrives in the thread
press 3: moves to s12
note.body:
Question two: where do we talk to them? Wherever the team already talks. Nobody in this building should have to learn a new tool to reach an agent, and nor should you.
(press)
Quick work goes in Slack. A colleague types a question in the channel where the talk already is, and tags at Rumi. That is all you do too: tag at Rumi in the channel, ask in plain words, and stay in the thread so the answer finds you.
(press)
The answer comes back in the same thread, from one name. Every agent below posts as Rumi, so the team only ever has one colleague to learn. Behind that face, the agents read Slack with a skill called slack-search and post with one called storytime, and storytime checks every post for internal details before it goes out. Keep Slack for short bursts, like a question or a quick yes. Anything that needs a long read belongs somewhere slower.
(press)
note.first_line: Question two: where do we talk to them?

cues: press 1: later, a link opens into a page in Notion
press 2: comments on the page; the change is made and resolved
press 3: moves to s13
note.body:
Deep work needs more room than a chat. A plan or a long review does not fit in a thread. Here the agent says where things stand, and the product manager says, let me know when you're done.
(press)
Later a link arrives, and it opens a page in Notion: a card on our To-do board, with the plan, the mockups and the open questions. Plans and reviews live there as cards, so you can find them again a month later. You work the board with your own Notion login; a card written as Rumi goes through the admin.
(press)
Then you work it the way you would with a colleague. Comment on the part you want changed and mention Rumi. The agent answers on the card and changes that part. Keep the talk on the card, so the reasoning stays with the work.
(press)
note.first_line: Deep work needs more room than a chat.

scenes.title: Google and email: the team's own files

cues: press 1: an email from Rumi lands
press 2: pull out to the building; one name above, many hands below
press 3: moves to s14
note.body:
Finished work lands where the team already keeps it: Docs, Sheets and Slides in a shared drive, where anyone on the team can open them and comment.
(press)
The agents on your Mac write Docs, Sheets and Slides into the team's shared drive. Anything sent as Rumi, from rumi at hellorumi dot ai, goes through the admin. Either way the work is never done at the first draft: the agent takes a picture of the page, reads it, fixes what looks wrong, and looks again.
(press)
So the team sees one colleague in Slack, in Notion and in the inbox. Below the floor, it is as many agents as the job needs, or one alone when one is enough. That answers question two.
(press)
note.first_line: Finished work lands where the team already keeps it: Docs, Sheets and Slides in a shared drive, where anyone on the team can open them and comment.

scenes.title: The note taker harvests what is said

cues: press 1: a meeting upstairs; the decision is said, then gone
press 2: the note taker is invited and joins as a tile
press 3: the words fall through the floor into the store
press 4: moves to s15
note.body:
Question three: how do they find out what is going on? A new colleague learns most of it by sitting in meetings.
(press)
Most of what we know is said out loud and never written down. Upstairs, a team agrees to add a practice step to every plan. Downstairs, nobody hears it, so the next plans are written the old way.
(press)
So we built our own note taker. Invite it to your call like any guest, Rumi note taker, and it joins as a tile. Do it for the weekly meeting, a call with a partner, even a call on your own to think out loud about a new build. We built it ourselves so that we decide how each meeting is kept.
(press)
Now the words fall through the floor and stay. About fourteen hundred and fifty meetings so far, each one where any agent can find it. A one-to-one is different: when someone asks in Slack, only the people who were in it can see it. So when you want the agents to know something, say it in a call the note taker is in.
(press)
note.first_line: Question three: how do they find out what is going on?

scenes.title: Read from the top: the tiers

cues: press 1: the layers named: one line, the summary, every word
press 2: a question in Slack; the light stops at one summary
press 3: pull back to the building; question three ticks
press 4: moves to s16
note.body:
About fourteen hundred and fifty meetings are no use if you have to read them whole. So here is the shape from the lesson-plan skill again: the overview first, the detail only when needed. We call it progressive disclosure.
(press)
Each meeting is kept in layers. On top, one line. Under it, the summary: who was there and what was decided. At the bottom, every word.
(press)
Ask what the lesson plans team decided last week. The agent reads the top lines of many meetings, opens one summary, and answers. It never opens the transcript. You can do the same with the meetings tool: search first, then the summary, and the transcript only when the summary cannot answer.
(press)
Our code is signposted the same way. The main folders each have a CLAUDE.md that says what is inside and where to go next: the root, then the folder, then the one document you need. Each agent arrives knowing nothing, so it finds its way from the root every time.
(press)
note.first_line: About fourteen hundred and fifty meetings are no use if you have to read them whole.

cues: press 1: one person works a lesson plan by hand; the page drops into the skills room
press 2: the skill, one page thicker, beside the cost paid once
press 3: one mark becomes a new line in the skill; 157 corrections
press 4: moves to s17
note.body:
Question four: does the work sound like us, and is it good enough? Most of what we know is in people's heads. Nobody wrote it down, so no agent can read it.
(press)
So the first time you do a job with an agent, do it by hand, together, and talk it through: why this activity, why this order, what you would never do. Then ask the agent to write the steps down as a skill. Say, make a skill for this, and the skill-authoring skill takes it from there.
(press)
That is amortisation. You pay to work the job out once, and every later job uses what you wrote. Before a new skill counts, it has to pass the skill lint, which checks it will load.
(press)
Then you correct its work, and each correction is a rule you did not know you had. Say, stop this happening again, and the agent-improvement skill writes the fix into the skill. Our lesson-plan skill numbers its fixes: a hundred and fifty-seven so far. One tip: before a long session ends, ask the agent to list every place you corrected it.
(press)

[Appendix: a03 the skills you use first. Press A, the number, Enter.]
note.first_line: Question four: does the work sound like us, and is it good enough?

scenes.title: Evals: a blind judge and a bar

cues: press 1: a page goes through a hatch into a small booth; an eval
press 2: inside the booth, the door to the makers is shut; a blind judge
press 3: the judge's note: a score, a reason, the quoted line
press 4: people's marks beside the judge's; a bar across the way out; one page goes back, comes again and clears; 1,953 of 2,038 lessons
press 5: moves to s18
note.body:
The second half of question four: is it good enough? Three hundred agents make more than anyone can read. But you have already written down what good looks like, in the skill.
(press)
So a second model marks the work against that standard. A check like this is called an eval; for people, it is an appraisal. Our lesson-plan reviewer, for example, scores on a hundred and eighty-four points and eight criteria. To build your own, use the evals skill.
(press)
The judge gets the work and the standard, and nothing else. It never sees the maker's notes or reasons, so nothing can talk it round. We call it a blind judge, like an external examiner.
(press)
Beside every score it writes its reason, and quotes the line it means. Read the reasons, not only the scores. When the same reason keeps coming back, the fix goes into the skill, and the next batch is better.
(press)
A judge is checked against people's marks on the same work before we trust it. Then the bar goes up: work under it goes back to its maker, and nothing counts as done until it clears. In one region, one thousand nine hundred and fifty-three of two thousand and thirty-eight lessons cleared a blind judge.
(press)
note.first_line: The second half of question four: is it good enough?

scenes.title: The harness, and the model you plug in

cues: press 1: the model lifts out and a different one drops in; question four ticks
press 2: moves to s19
note.body:
Pull back and look at the whole lower floor: the board, the skills, the hooks, the note taker, the judges. All of it sits around the model, and together it has a name: the harness. You build it a rule and a skill at a time, and it is ours to keep.
(press)
The model is the part we rent. When a better one comes out, it plugs into the same harness and nothing else changes. Before you switch, run it past the same judges and the same bar, so you know it is better instead of hoping. In the early days, a strong model makes up for a thin harness. Once the harness is strong, a cheaper model can often do the job.
(press)
note.first_line: Pull back and look at the whole lower floor: the board, the skills, the hooks, the note taker, the judges.

cues: press 1: a person comes down the stairs, checks the lit places in turn, and the stuck lane flows; "an operator, the person who runs the agents"
press 2: back out to the whole building, "an operator" beside the person at the hatch
press 3: moves to s20
note.body:
Question five: what happens when the volume grows? With hundreds of agents at work, some get stuck. One meets a case nobody wrote down, another loops on the same job, and the work behind it stops. One lane is jammed, and from upstairs nobody can see why.
(press)
Someone has to know where to look. That person is the operator, and from this week the operator is you. You create the agents, you brief them, and you unblock them. When one stalls, you check four places in turn: the judge's score, the code, the data, and the release. Most jams clear at one of those four, and the lane starts to flow again.
(press)
So the operator is the first role an organisation needs when it brings agents in: from day one. The rest of this part of the show is about doing that job well while the work keeps growing, by day and by night.
[Presenter, in your own words: what it felt like the first time you unblocked an agent yourself.]
(press)
note.first_line: Question five: what happens when the volume grows?

scenes.title: Agent teams and the red team

cues: press 1: one agent under one long card becomes five round a board; one holds a red pencil and marks a note; "an agent team"
press 2: a real team board scrolls: kinds of post, roles, no names
press 3: moves to s21
note.body:
As the volume grows, one agent working alone on a big job becomes the bottleneck. It is slow, and nobody argues with it, so its mistakes go out sounding sure of themselves.
(press)
So big jobs go to a team. A chief of staff and a lead decide; managers each run a few agents; everyone posts on one shared board, and the work moves in gated rounds. One member, the red team, has a single job: find the faults. It holds the red pencil and sends work back. A panel and a quality check stand at the end.
(press)
This is a real team board: the agents writing to each other, ready, finding, sent back. You set a team off with the agent-team skill, and you hear only what is yours to decide: a production go, or a call the brief does not settle. Our October town hall show was built overnight by a thirty-lane agent team, and this show was built the same way.
(press)

[Appendix: a10 the Agent Management team. Press A, the number, Enter.]
note.first_line: As the volume grows, one agent working alone on a big job becomes the bottleneck.

cues: press 1: envelopes pass from agent to agent and land in each other's inboxes
press 2: back out to the whole building at night; the people upstairs go home; the floors work on
press 3: morning; back into the room; the staging door lights and opens; an agent shows the work; the operator looks
press 4: the operator tests on the phone; the two end-to-end checks tick
press 5: the production door lights and opens on the operator's go; the agents hop
press 6: moves to s22
note.body:
Here is how agents work at night. You sit at the centre, and around you is a team of agents, a swarm. You give each one a piece of the work with a clear brief, and it gets on with it.
(press)
Each agent has an inbox. They pass each other short, plain messages: this part is done, please check that one. You can read every message.
(press)
So you can leave the swarm on overnight. You go offline, the people upstairs go home, and the work goes on, floor by floor. Brief it well before you log off, because the brief is most of your work that night.
(press)
In the morning it shows you what it built, on staging. Staging is a test copy of the bot on its own WhatsApp number, so no teacher talks to it. On the main bot it shares the production database, so a database change there reaches production too. You open it and look at the work yourself.
(press)
Then one rule with no exceptions. Before anything ships, test it end to end, the way a teacher would meet it: send the messages yourself on WhatsApp, or run the browser tests. Green unit tests do not count as a working bot.
(press)
When you have seen it work and you are happy, it goes to production, the real bot that teachers use. That go is yours, and you give it fresh every time, even when you agreed the plan the day before.
(press)

[Appendix: a04 how a change reaches production. Press A, the number, Enter.]
note.first_line: Here is how agents work at night.

cues: press 1: the notice runs down to the small lit box, and one sleeping agent wakes
press 2: three calls arrive in turn, each wakes one agent; "reactive"
press 3: a clock: 25 minutes before the meeting; the note taker gets up by itself and writes a brief with sources
press 4: in the call, its tile raises a hand and its point appears in the chat
press 5: back out to the building; the note taker's tile is the one lit thing among the sleepers; "From reactive to proactive"
press 6: moves to s23
note.body:
The agents that answer the team's questions should not run all day, so they sleep until someone needs them. When you tag @Rumi in a Slack channel, or comment to Rumi on a Notion card, that system sends a notice called a webhook. It reaches a small service that never sleeps.
(press)
That service wakes the one agent the request is for. It does the work and answers where it was asked; the rest sleep on. A hook stops an action; a webhook wakes an agent.
(press)
Notice one thing about every agent you have met so far. Each one waits to be asked. That kind of agent is called reactive.
(press)
The next step is proactive. Before each of our internal meetings, the note taker gets up by itself. It reads past meetings, the team chat, Notion and our product data, and writes a short brief with a source and a date on every point. It reads only meetings marked public; one-to-ones stay private to their people.
(press)
In the meeting, when it has a point worth making, it raises its hand. Its point appears in the chat, and it speaks only when it is invited.
(press)
An agent that acts before anyone asks is called proactive: it spots a gap and tells you.
(press)
note.first_line: The agents that answer the team's questions should not run all day, so they sleep until someone needs them.

cues: press 1: the camera closes on the first card: what you see
press 2: the next card: why, in the teacher's own words
press 3: the next card: what might help, and when
press 4: the last card: if… then…, and what would prove it wrong
press 5: pull back to the whole board; the lesson-plan example beside it, with what would prove it wrong
press 6: the row turns over: quizzes at home, with what would prove it wrong
press 7: moves to s24
note.body:
Ship on a hypothesis, not an opinion, and work it out with the full-stack builders in your region, the FSBs.
A team will often want to ship because someone feels sure. Your job is to ask for a hypothesis instead. The FSBs are the people who build what you ship. You settle each hypothesis with them and make sure the process is kept. A hypothesis has four ingredients.
(press)
One: what you see. The number, and where it is low.
(press)
Two: why it happens. The teacher's reason, in their own words. Did a teacher tell us this, or are we guessing?
(press)
Three: what might help. The change, and the date teachers get it.
(press)
Four: if this, then that, because. Then write down the result that would prove you wrong, before you ship.
(press)
Here is one from September. What we saw: lesson plans ran to eleven to sixteen pages. Why: teachers read them on a phone. What might help: pages made for the phone, and they came down to five to nine. If we do that, then more plans get used. We are wrong if the share of teachers making a plan each day does not rise in the RDF, each region's weekly charts.
(press)

Every region has a huddle every day: a short meeting, standing, with the regional manager, the field team, the FSBs and you. Visit a school once a fortnight. It is mandatory.
A visit is where you see Teach Well, Improve and Learn happen in a real room. Run the school-visits skill before you go: it pulls the school's history together and tells you whom to observe and what to ask. In the classroom, sit at the back and watch the board and the lesson as it is taught. That is Teach Well.

Improve is the conversation with the teacher afterwards: what helped them today, and what got in the way.
